title: For Dalit People to Know!
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement. Letter-specific notes: 1. The intentional English headline from *The Hindu* is retained exactly as printed in the audited Tamil source. 2. `lakh` is retained as an Indian public-language numbering unit. 3. Community names are rendered closely to the source; the translation does not modernise or reconcile the source's varying caste/community terminology.
paragraphs: The very day after the 2013–2014 Budget was read in the Assembly, a special correspondent of Dinamalar wrote that those disappointed that the Budget contained no major projects, announcements, freebies or concession schemes should wait patiently until 1 April, because Chief Minister Jayalalithaa could certainly be expected to set off a string of dramatic announcements under Assembly Rule 110. When we compare that prediction with the Chief Minister now reading out, from 1 April onward, announcement after announcement concerning each department under Rule 110, we can understand how accurately Dinamalar had anticipated the extent to which the AIADMK Chief Minister is interested in making announcements.

Speak critically of the Chief Minister or the government in the Assembly and there is immediate expulsion; yesterday even the principal opposition party was denied the opportunity to open the debate on a demand for grants. This is how matters continue. Tamil Nadu's newspapers are afraid to condemn all this. They seem to think: why invite trouble? It was in this situation that this morning (10 April 2013) The Hindu carried a report by its special correspondent under the headline, “Atrocities against Dalits touched their peak in 2012, finds study.”

The report said that atrocities against Dalits reached their highest level in fifteen years in 2012; Villupuram, Virudhunagar, Dharmapuri and Theni recorded the greatest number of atrocities. The study was conducted by the Madurai-based voluntary organisation Evidence. Compensation and rehabilitation legally due to victims had not yet reached them, except in the Dharmapuri incident. Of 370 incidents studied, 112 occurred in 2012 alone and involved attacks on Dalits; 28 had very grave consequences; Dalit homes were set ablaze in 36 incidents; 96 incidents ending in murder had resulted in cases that remained pending before courts, with convictions in only three. Sexual offences against Dalit women were reported in 62 incidents; cases had been filed in all of them, but not one had yet resulted in punishment.

Thus, a voluntary organisation has studied the matter and declared that such atrocities against Dalits occurred at their highest level in 2012 under AIADMK rule. What suffering awaits the organisation that has given this government such a certificate?

During DMK rule, however, wherever an atrocity against Dalits occurred, immediate action was taken and the situation brought under control. Intelligence was also used to identify where atrocities might occur so that preventive measures could be taken. I consider it my duty to give just a few examples.

At Uthapuram in Peraiyur taluk of Madurai district, a dispute had arisen in 1990 between the Pillaimar community and Adi Dravidars. With the aim of maintaining law, order and peace, both communities were brought to agreement and, in accordance with an agreement already reached in 1989, a 103-metre protective wall was constructed between the two residential areas on behalf of the Vellalar community association.

A peace meeting was held on 2 May 2008 to resolve issues arising from Adi Dravidar demands to remove the wall, create access through the pathway in the area where the Vellalar community lived, and remove the compound wall around the temple and peepal tree in accordance with the 1989 agreement. As a settlement was about to be reached, Adi Dravidars insisted that the wall beside the Mariamman temple be removed under the written 1989 agreement. The District Revenue Officer inspected the disputed lands with the subordinate official and, after obtaining legal opinion on 4 May 2008, a portion of the wall was broken on 6 May to create a path connecting the existing panchayat road to the area where Adi Dravidars predominantly lived.

Following recommendations of the government-appointed inquiry committee into the dispute, the DMK government issued an order on 12 September 2009 sanctioning ₹10.28 lakh in assistance to 191 people, and the money was distributed on 15 and 16 September.

In Uthapuram, assistance also included ₹16,000 as marriage aid to four families; ₹87,500 for natural deaths and funeral rites; ₹20,000 under the Destitute Assistance Scheme to two widowed women; and monthly assistance of ₹400 to a total of 113 elderly people, widows, deserted women, persons with disabilities, agricultural labourers and beneficiaries under the Indira Gandhi National Old Age scheme. Free colour television sets were provided to 1,655 families at a cost of ₹38,41,255; free gas stoves with connections to 80 families at ₹2.32 lakh; 2.03 hectares of land to eight people valued at ₹60,515; and free house sites to 35 families valued at ₹10,870.

In addition, works worth ₹39.33 lakh were carried out in the north street where the Vellalar community lived, including an overhead water tank, culvert, cement road, marriage hall, a house under the Indira Memorial Housing Scheme, streetlights, cremation-ground compound wall, drinking-water facilities, roads, library building and playground.

Similarly, in the south street inhabited by Adi Dravidars, works costing ₹73.23 lakh included a nutritious-meal centre building, tar and cement roads, roofs at cremation grounds, a threshing floor, a compound wall for the government middle school, drainage, drinking water and streetlights; 40 houses under the Indira Housing Scheme and 14 kutcha houses; a drama stage, bathing tank, community hall and roads.

At Kangeyanur in Villupuram district, after a man named Kubendran of the Adi Dravidar community of Melanthal alleged that he had been attacked on 8 August 2009 following the previous day's fire-walking festival at the Draupadi Amman temple, about 90 residents of Melanthal Colony blocked the Moongilthuraipattu road with thorns and timber. A dispute arose between the two sections and an inquiry was ordered by the Tirukkoyilur Revenue Divisional Officer. Following a peace committee meeting conducted by the Villupuram District Revenue Officer, the temple was opened on 7 October 2009 and people of all sections from Kangeyanur, Mettucheri and Melanthal worshipped there.

At Chettipulam in Vedaranyam taluk of Nagapattinam district, a dispute over Adi Dravidars entering the locked Kamatchi Amman temple created the possibility of unrest. Peace talks were therefore held at the Nagapattinam Revenue Divisional Office on 8 October 2009. It was agreed that all villagers would enter and worship at 11 a.m. on 14 October. With police assistance, the situation was controlled and law and order maintained.

At Kannanallur Mariamman temple in Panthapuli village, Sankarankovil taluk, Tirunelveli district, a dispute arose over worship between caste Hindus and Devendrakula Vellalars. In litigation brought by the two communities, the Sankarankovil District Munsif Court ruled on 11 August 2008 that the temple did not belong exclusively to any particular community. On that basis, members of the Scheduled Castes sought permission to conduct the Kodai festival on 23 September 2008. Because of the tense situation, a peace committee meeting was held under the District Revenue Officer. Later, following my advice, the temple was opened under heavy security on 24 December 2008 so that all communities could worship together, and members of the oppressed community entered and worshipped.

For many years, elections had not been held and local democratic processes had not functioned in the four panchayats of Keeripatti, Pappapatti and Nattarmangalam in Madurai district and Kottakachiyendal in Virudhunagar district, because reservation meant that only members of the Dalit community could contest there. After the DMK government took office in 2006, peaceful elections were held in all four panchayats during the October local-body elections with the cooperation of every community. Members were elected, creating a new history of social harmony.

To honour the leaders, elected representatives and people of the various communities who made that achievement possible, a major felicitation called the “Samathuva Peruvizha” was held in Chennai on 13 November 2006. Speaking there, I announced ₹20 lakh from the Tamil Nadu government for each panchayat—₹80 lakh in all—to improve basic amenities, and ₹5 lakh from the DMK for each—₹20 lakh in all. Those amounts were provided accordingly.

I have placed before you both examples of how atrocities affecting Dalit people were addressed through dialogue during DMK rule and a documented news report showing the extent to which that community is now subjected to atrocities under AIADMK rule. I am confident that Dalit people themselves will understand clearly how the situation was handled under the two governments.
